Principle 18: The Traditional Holidays of Korea
An Introduction to the Traditional Holidays of Korea
What is a holiday? Holidays are special times (of the year) when families get together and celebrate.
Many holidays are known worldwide such as New Year’s Day and Christmas, but most holidays are celebrated by certain cultures.
These kinds of holidays are called traditional holidays.
Korea has many traditional holidays, but the two largest ones are Lunar New Year’s and Chuseok.
Lunar New Year’s (설날)
The first big holiday is Lunar New Year’s, which is also known as Seollal.
It is celebrated on the first day of the first month on the lunar calendar.
The most important Lunar New Year’s custom is the ancestral memorial rites ceremony.
Each member of the family gets up early in the morning and dresses in their best clothes.
During this ceremony, Koreans perform a ritual ceremony in honor of their ancestors.
Following the ceremony, the youth bow to their elders as a gesture of wishing everyone many new blessings during the upcoming new year.
To bow on the Lunar New Year is a special honor and privilege of showing respect to one’s elders.
Chuseok (추석)
Chuseok is the biggest national holiday of the year, and it is often referred to as the Korean Thanksgiving.
It is celebrated on the fifteenth day of the eighth month on the lunar calendar.
During Chuseok, Koreans visit their ancestral tombs and make an offering of food to their ancestors.
Most people play games with their relatives such as yut-nori, which is a traditional game played with four rounded wooden sticks;
others make song-pyeun, which is a Korean traditional rice cake eaten especially during Chuseok.
I like our country’s traditional holidays because it is a time when all family members gather together to celebrate life.
On these days, I learn how important family really is!
